title: Vectors are more than arrows
learningObjective: Recognize a real vector space by its operations and axioms.

retrieve.bodyMarkdown: Recall how to add ordered pairs and multiply each coordinate by a real number. No calculus is needed; familiarity with elementary algebra and the idea of a proof is enough.

encounter.bodyMarkdown: An arrow, a polynomial, and a list of sensor readings look different. What lets the same rules describe all three?

explain.bodyMarkdown: A real vector space has addition and multiplication by real scalars. Addition is associative and commutative, has a zero vector and additive inverses. Scalars satisfy $a(bv)=(ab)v$, $1v=v$, $a(u+v)=au+av$, and $(a+b)v=av+bv$. Operations must stay inside the set. Polynomials of degree at most two, including the zero polynomial, form $P_2$: adding them cannot create a higher-degree term. Polynomials of degree exactly two do not form a vector space. The zero vector need not look like a list of zeros; in a function space it is the function that is zero everywhere.

figure.caption: In ℝ², u + v is found tip-to-tail — the same addition rule that must hold in any vector space.

reflect.bodyMarkdown: The objects do not determine whether a set is a vector space: the operations and closure do. A single failed axiom is enough to refute a claim.

problems.promptMarkdown: Which set is a real vector space with the usual polynomial operations?

options.label: Polynomials of degree at most two, including zero.
options.accessibleLabel: Polynomials of degree at most two, including zero.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Check which set contains the additive identity.
A vector space must be closed under every real scalar.
Multiplication by zero tests two of the options immediately.
Degree at most two is preserved by sums and scalar multiples, and includes the zero polynomial. The other sets exclude zero.

problems.solutionMarkdown: Degree at most two is preserved by sums and scalar multiples, and includes the zero polynomial. The other sets exclude zero.

problems.promptMarkdown: In $\mathbb R^2$, let $u=(2,-1)$ and $v=(-1,3)$. What is the second coordinate of $2u+v$?

figure.caption: u and v, ready to be scaled and added.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Track only the requested coordinate.
Scalar multiplication acts on each coordinate.
The second coordinate is $2(-1)+3$.
Compute coordinatewise: $2u+v=(4,-2)+(-1,3)=(3,1)$. The second coordinate is $1$.

problems.solutionMarkdown: Compute coordinatewise: $2u+v=(4,-2)+(-1,3)=(3,1)$. The second coordinate is $1$.

problems.promptMarkdown: Let $S=\{(x,y):x>0\}$ with ordinary operations. Which is a valid reason it is not a real vector space?

options.label: It contains vectors of different lengths.
options.accessibleLabel: It contains vectors of different lengths.

options.label: It does not contain the zero vector.
options.accessibleLabel: It does not contain the zero vector.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Find a required element missing from the set.
Every vector space contains an additive identity.
Check the inequality at $(0,0)$.
The zero vector has first coordinate zero, so it is not in $S$. Infinitely many elements and different lengths cause no problem.

problems.solutionMarkdown: The zero vector has first coordinate zero, so it is not in $S$. Infinitely many elements and different lengths cause no problem.

problems.promptMarkdown: Complete the scalar distributive law: $(a+b)v=\boxed{\phantom{a}}v+\boxed{\phantom{b}}v$. Enter the scalar in each blank.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Identify the coefficients on the two copies of the vector.
Distribute multiplication across scalar addition.
One term uses the first scalar and the other uses the second.
The law is $(a+b)v=av+bv$. It links addition of scalars to addition of vectors.

problems.solutionMarkdown: The law is $(a+b)v=av+bv$. It links addition of scalars to addition of vectors.

problems.promptMarkdown: Arrange this proof that the additive identity is unique.

steps.textMarkdown: Suppose $z$ and $w$ are both additive identities.
Because $z$ is an identity, the same sum $z+w=w$.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Show that any two proposed identities are equal.
Use each identity on the same sum.
Evaluate $z+w$ using first $w$, then $z$.
Compare the same sum in two ways. The defining property of each identity forces the sum to equal both of them, so they coincide.

problems.solutionMarkdown: Compare the same sum in two ways. The defining property of each identity forces the sum to equal both of them, so they coincide.
